newsitem.title: USA: U.S. air quality getting better, EPA says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. air quality getting better, EPA says.

text.p: The nation's air is about 30 percent cleaner than 25 years ago, with the most dramatic declines in the sulphur dioxide emissions that contribute to acid rain, the Environmental Protection Agency said Tuesday.

In its annual report on air quality trends, covering data through 1995, the EPA said 1995's unusually hot summer caused a temporary increase in smog levels. But the improvement over the 1980s continued since last year's peak smog concentrations were 16 percent below levels in 1988, another unusually hot summer, it said.

"Over 25 years, the gross domestic product increased 99 percent while emissions of the nation's six major pollutants declined by 29 percent," EPA Administrator Carol Browner told a news conference. "Economic growth and environmental protection can go hand in hand," she said.

The EPA reported that increased use of cleaner-burning reformulated gasoline contributed to a sizable drop in the concentration of a number of toxic air pollutants, particularly benzene, which fell 38 percent in 1995 from 1994.

The concentration of carbon monoxide, mainly from automobile exhaust, fell 10 percent between 1994 and 1995, its biggest year-to-year drop. Sulphur dioxide concentration, which fell 37 percent over 10 years, dropped 17 percent from 1994 to 1995 as more controls were put on coal-fired electric power plants under the programme to curb acid rain.

The report was released as the Clinton administration was pushing tougher standards against smog and soot, which it said must be strengthened to protect about 50 million people at risk from lung diseases such as asthma.

"As science provides us with new information about the health risks of air pollution, EPA must continually review and update our national standards to ensure that they protect the public," Browner said.

But industry groups have said tighter standards against smog-forming ozone and soot, or airborne particles that may lodge in the lungs, will yield only marginal public health benefits while taking a dramatic toll on the economy by suppressing industrial growth.

Despite the overall improvement in air quality, the EPA said 80 million people lived in counties that did not meet the air quality standard for at least one pollutant in 1995. Urban smog remained the biggest problem, it said.
